description: Protein, fats and carbohydrates: functions, sources, essential amino acids and fat classification.
content_html:
Defining Macronutrients

The spec gives a precise definition that examiners expect you to reproduce: macronutrients are “a class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities.” There are three: protein, fats (lipids), and carbohydrates. These are the nutrients you eat in gram-sized amounts every day — contrasted with micronutrients (vitamins, minerals), which are needed in milligram or microgram quantities. Getting this definition word-for-word correct is a reliable early mark on any principles of nutrition question.

Key Fact

Energy values to memorise: protein provides 4 kcal per gram; carbohydrate provides 4 kcal per gram; fat provides 9 kcal per gram. Fat is more than double the energy density of the other two macronutrients — relevant when planning diets for athletes (high energy needs) or those managing weight.

Protein: Essential and Non-Essential Amino Acids

Proteins are chains of amino acids. There are twenty amino acids in total, but the spec focuses on the split between essential and non-essential. Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from food. The nine on the spec are: histidine, isoleucine, lysine, leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. Non-essential amino acids — including alanine, asparagine, aspartic acid and glutamic acid — can be synthesised by the body from other compounds.

Foods that contain all nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts are called high biological-value (HBV) proteins. Animal foods — meat, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy — are HBV. Most plant proteins are low biological-value (LBV) because they lack one or more essential amino acids. Soya and quinoa are notable exceptions — both are complete plant proteins. For a 14-year-old vegan athlete, combining lentil curry with brown rice at dinner provides a complete amino acid profile, because lentils are low in methionine (plentiful in rice) and rice is low in lysine (plentiful in lentils).

The primary functions of protein are: growth and repair of body tissues; production of enzymes, hormones and antibodies; and as a secondary energy source (the body uses protein for energy when carbohydrate stores are depleted). Recommended daily intake for adults is approximately 0.75 g per kg of body weight — higher for adolescents, pregnant women and those recovering from illness or surgery.

Fats, Oils and Lipids

Dietary fats are classified by their chemical structure — specifically by the number of double bonds between carbon atoms in their fatty acid chains. Saturated fats have no double bonds and tend to be solid at room temperature. They are found mainly in animal products (butter, lard, fatty meat, full-fat dairy, palm oil) and are associated with raised LDL (“bad”) cholesterol and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) when consumed in excess. Monounsaturated fats have one double bond. Olive oil, rapeseed oil, avocados and most nuts are rich in monounsaturated fats; they are associated with a more favourable cholesterol profile.

Polyunsaturated fats have two or more double bonds. This category includes the essential fatty acids — omega-3 (alpha-linolenic acid) and omega-6 (linoleic acid) — which cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained from food. Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) are the richest source of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, which support brain function, reduce inflammation, and lower triglyceride levels. Vegetable oils such as sunflower and corn oil are high in omega-6. The current dietary advice is to increase omega-3 intake and moderate omega-6, since Western diets tend to be omega-6 heavy.

The functions of dietary fat extend beyond energy: fat carries and enables absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; provides insulation for organs; and supplies essential fatty acids that the body cannot make. A diet very low in fat may therefore lead to deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins even if those vitamins are consumed — because without fat, they cannot be absorbed in the small intestine.

High intake of saturated fat → raised LDL cholesterol in the blood → LDL deposits on artery walls → formation of plaques (atherosclerosis) → narrowed arteries → increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) or stroke. The key vocabulary to use in an exam: saturated fat, LDL cholesterol, atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease. A student who writes “saturated fat causes heart disease” scores 1 mark; a student who writes the full chain using this vocabulary scores much more in an extended response.

Carbohydrates: Monosaccharides, Disaccharides and Polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred energy source. They are classified by the number of sugar units they contain. Monosaccharides are single sugar units: glucose (found in fruit and honey; the form of sugar the body uses for energy), fructose (fruit sugar) and galactose (found in milk). Disaccharides are two monosaccharides bonded together: sucrose (glucose + fructose — table sugar), lactose (glucose + galactose — milk sugar), and maltose (glucose + glucose — from malt). Polysaccharides are long chains of glucose units. Starch (from plants: potatoes, flour, rice) and glycogen (stored in the liver and muscle) are digestible polysaccharides. Non-starch polysaccharides (NSP) — dietary fibre — are not digested in the small intestine, passing instead to the colon where they feed beneficial bacteria and support bowel health.

Starchy polysaccharides release energy more slowly than simple sugars because they require digestion before glucose enters the bloodstream. This is why a bowl of porridge oats before a 5 km run sustains energy better than a spoonful of sugar — the polysaccharide structure means glucose is absorbed gradually, maintaining a stable blood sugar level rather than a rapid spike and crash. This is particularly important for managing type 2 diabetes, where the glycaemic response to food is a key dietary concern.

Key Fact

Monosaccharides: glucose, fructose, galactose. Disaccharides: sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), maltose. Polysaccharides: starch, glycogen, non-starch polysaccharides (dietary fibre). The written paper can ask students to classify a named carbohydrate — knowing which group each falls into is a reliable recall mark.

Malnutrition means ‘wrong nutrition’ in either direction — too much or too little. Protein deficiency causes stunted growth, poor wound healing, muscle wasting and impaired immunity; in severe global poverty, the condition kwashiorkor (characterised by oedema) can develop. Excess protein puts strain on the kidneys, which must excrete the nitrogenous waste. Excess saturated fat raises CVD risk and contributes to obesity; fat deficiency impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption and disrupts hormone production. Excess refined carbohydrate / free sugars contributes to type 2 diabetes, dental caries and obesity; insufficient carbohydrate causes fatigue and forces the body to break down protein and fat for energy, producing ketones. For the exam, tie each consequence to a named individual (e.g. an obese adult, a vegan with inadequate protein, a child with dental caries) to access AO2 application marks.
exam_tip_html: On the 8-mark Discuss / Analyse question, students most often present only one perspective. The command word ‘Discuss’ means ‘present, analyse and consider relevant points’ — multiple perspectives are expected. For a macronutrient question (for example, analysing the role of fat in the diet), a top-band response would discuss: (1) the positive functions of fat (energy, fat-soluble vitamin absorption, essential fatty acids, insulation); and (2) the negative effects of excess saturated fat intake (raised LDL cholesterol, atherosclerosis, CVD risk). Use named technical vocabulary throughout: saturated fat, monounsaturated, polyunsaturated, LDL cholesterol, atherosclerosis, essential fatty acids. Without this vocabulary, answers tend to cap at Developing or Secure even when the underlying reasoning is sound. A quick self-check: “Have I named at least two different perspectives? Have I used at least three technical terms? Have I linked each point to the named eater or context in the question?”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Macronutrients are “chemical compounds consumed in the largest quantities” — protein, fats and carbohydrates. The nine essential amino acids (histidine, isoleucine, lysine, leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine) cannot be made by the body and must come from food.
  • Fats are classified as saturated (solid at room temperature, animal sources, linked to CVD), monounsaturated (olive oil, avocado), or polyunsaturated (including essential omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids). Essential fatty acids must come from food, as the body cannot make them.
  • Carbohydrates fall into three groups: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, NSP). Polysaccharides release energy slowly, making them the better fuel for sustained activity and blood-sugar stability.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct spec definition of macronutrients?
A) Nutrients required in small quantities to facilitate physiological functions
B) A class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities
C) Nutrients the body cannot synthesise and must obtain from food
D) Compounds that provide more than 5 kcal of energy per gram
practice_questions.marks: B) A class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the nine essential amino acids that the spec requires you to know.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming any four; 2 marks for naming all nine correctly: histidine, isoleucine, lysine, leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine. [Note: This tests recall of the full list. Partial credit at 1 mark for 4-8 correct; 2 marks for all nine.]

practice_questions.text: Describe the three classifications of carbohydrates with one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per classification correctly named and described with an example, up to 3 marks. Monosaccharides: single sugar units — examples: glucose, fructose, galactose (1). Disaccharides: two monosaccharide units joined together — examples: sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), maltose (1). Polysaccharides: long chains of glucose units — examples: starch, glycogen, non-starch polysaccharides / dietary fibre (1).

practice_questions.text: Tavita, age 17, is a competitive swimmer who trains six days a week. His sports nutritionist advises him to prioritise complex carbohydrates rather than simple sugars in his pre-training meals. Explain why this advice is appropriate for Tavita.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per explanation (1 for the point, 1 for a linked reason), up to 4 marks. Complex carbohydrates (polysaccharides such as starch) release glucose more gradually than simple sugars, because they require longer digestion, which means that Tavita's blood glucose level stays stable over the duration of training rather than spiking then dropping (2). Stable blood glucose maintains energy output over long training sessions, because glucose is the preferred fuel for high-intensity exercise and if blood glucose drops Tavita will fatigue prematurely and performance will decline (2). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the positive and negative effects of fat in the diet, with reference to the different types of dietary fat.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced discussion of both positive and negative effects with explicit reference to saturated, monounsaturated AND polyunsaturated fats plus essential fatty acids. Named functions of fat (energy, fat-soluble vitamin absorption, essential fatty acids, insulation, hormone production). Negative effects trace the saturated fat pathway (LDL cholesterol, atherosclerosis, CVD). At least one perspective is developed in depth. Accurate use of technical vocabulary throughout. Secure (5-6 marks): Both positive and negative effects covered; at least two fat types named; mostly accurate with some development. Links between diet and health outcomes present but not fully developed. Developing (3-4 marks): One perspective more developed than the other; some accurate nutritional knowledge; limited use of technical vocabulary; minimal cause-and-effect chains. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic facts about fat stated; no distinction between fat types; single perspective only. Indicative positive content: energy (9 kcal/g); carries fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K; essential fatty acids (omega-3, omega-6) cannot be made by the body and support brain function and reduce inflammation; monounsaturated fat (olive oil) associated with favourable cholesterol profile; fat provides insulation and protects organs. Indicative negative content: excess saturated fat (butter, lard, fatty meat) raises LDL cholesterol; LDL deposits on artery walls as plaques (atherosclerosis); raises risk of coronary heart disease and stroke; excess fat intake contributes to obesity and type 2 diabetes.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by protein complementation and give one example of how it works in a meal.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for explaining the concept (1 for defining LBV plant proteins as lacking one or more essential amino acids, 1 for explaining that combining two LBV sources provides all nine essential amino acids). 2 marks for a worked meal example (1 for naming two specific foods, 1 for explaining which amino acids each contributes or for explaining why together they form a complete protein). Example answer: most plant proteins are low biological-value because they lack one or more essential amino acids (1); combining two LBV plant proteins in the same meal means their complementary amino acid profiles together provide all nine essential amino acids the body needs (1); for example, red lentil dhal (low in methionine) served with basmati rice (low in lysine) — the methionine from the rice and the lysine from the lentils together give a complete protein (2).

Sucrose is a _____ made from one molecule of glucose joined to one molecule of fructose.
Which type of fat is found mainly in oily fish and is classed as an essential fatty acid?

flashcard_questions.q: What is the spec definition of macronutrients?
flashcard_questions.a: A class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the nine essential amino acids.
flashcard_questions.a: Histidine, isoleucine, lysine, leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine.
It contains all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the energy value of fat per gram?
What is the difference between saturated and unsaturated fats?
flashcard_questions.a: Saturated fats have no double bonds (solid at room temperature); unsaturated fats have one or more double bonds (liquid at room temperature).
Polyunsaturated fats (omega-3 and omega-6) the body cannot make, so they must come from food.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a monosaccharide? Give two examples.
flashcard_questions.a: A single sugar unit. Examples: glucose, fructose, galactose.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a disaccharide? Give two examples.
flashcard_questions.a: Two monosaccharide units joined together. Examples: sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar).

flashcard_questions.q: What is a polysaccharide? Give two examples.
flashcard_questions.a: A long chain of glucose units. Examples: starch, glycogen, dietary fibre (NSP).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does excess saturated fat intake increase CVD risk?
flashcard_questions.a: It raises LDL cholesterol, which deposits on artery walls as plaques (atherosclerosis), narrowing arteries.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is starch a better pre-exercise food than simple sugar?
flashcard_questions.a: Starch (polysaccharide) releases glucose slowly, maintaining stable blood sugar; simple sugar causes a rapid spike then drop.

glossary_terms.definition: A class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities: protein, fats and carbohydrates.
Amino acids the body cannot synthesise and must obtain from food: histidine, isoleucine, lysine, leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine.
Fats with no double bonds in their fatty acid chains, solid at room temperature, found mainly in animal products and associated with raised LDL cholesterol.
Fats with two or more double bonds in their fatty acid chains, including omega-3 and omega-6 essential fatty acids, found in oily fish and vegetable oils.
The simplest form of carbohydrate: single sugar units including glucose, fructose and galactose.
Carbohydrates formed from two monosaccharide units joined together, including sucrose, lactose and maltose.
Long chains of glucose units, including digestible forms (starch, glycogen) and non-digestible forms (non-starch polysaccharides/dietary fibre).
The combination of two low biological-value plant proteins in a meal so that together they supply all nine essential amino acids.

hero_image_caption: Protein, fats and carbohydrates — the three macronutrients consumed in the largest quantities — each play distinct roles in fuelling and maintaining the body.
